key_features.classic_presentation: ONSET: SUDDEN, DRAMATIC onset within minutes. Acute, catastrophic presentation. LOCATION: Initially EPIGASTRIC (perforated ulcer) or localized, then becomes DIFFUSE as peritonitis develops. May have shoulder pain (diaphragmatic irritation). DURATION: CONSTANT from onset. Unrelenting, persists continuously. CHARACTER: SUDDEN, SEVERE, SHARP pain described as 'STABBED' or 'KICKED'. Excruciating, worst pain imaginable. AGGRAVATING: ANY MOVEMENT worsens pain dramatically. Breathing, coughing, talking all worsen. Jarring or bumps unbearable. RELIEVING: NOTHING helps. Patient lies PERFECTLY STILL. Position doesn't relieve. Requires emergency surgery. TIMING: CONSTANT and unrelenting from onset. Progressive worsening as peritonitis spreads. SEVERITY: 10/10, maximal severity. Catastrophic pain. ASSOCIATED SYMPTOMS: Nausea, vomiting, inability to pass gas, fever develops after 6-12 hours. BOARD-LIKE RIGID ABDOMEN, absent bowel sounds. KEY POSITIVES: Rigid abdomen, severe rebound, patient perfectly still, sudden onset, prior ulcer/NSAID use. KEY NEGATIVES: SOFT abdomen rules out. Gradual onset suggests alternative. SURGICAL EMERGENCY - call 911.

red_flags: SURGICAL EMERGENCY - rigid abdomen with severe pain - call 911 immediately
Hypotension or tachycardia - septic shock from peritonitis
Free air under diaphragm on x-ray - confirmatory for perforation
ANY delay in treatment increases mortality - needs emergency surgery
